title: Length

findings.finding: The mixed-unit example substitutes 35 for the labelled 3.5 cm without stating the conversion.
findings.breakdown: The decisive common-unit conversion is absent from the written demonstration.
findings.checked: p5-information, p5-conversion-diagram and p5-guided teach conversion. Nevertheless, p10-units-example-entry does not connect its diagram label to the substituted value, as the worked-example standard requires.
findings.assumptions: Students have completed the units topic. Calculator availability does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Before the perimeter calculation, add: 'Use millimetres: 3.5 cm = 3.5 × 10 mm = 35 mm.'

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly connects 3.5 cm to the 35 mm used in its perimeter sum.

findings.finding: The overlapping rectangles require deriving unlabelled boundary lengths before the booklet teaches how to do this.
findings.breakdown: The two inner edges require 8 − 3 = 5 cm. Earlier examples supply boundary lengths directly or through equality marks; they do not connect overall dimensions with missing rectilinear sides.
findings.checked: Checked the polygon teaching and p11-q1 through p14-q10. None demonstrates the required subtraction. The later p16-l-shapes-missing-side-explanation, identification activity and p17-example-content supply exactly this method.
findings.assumptions: Elementary subtraction and rectangle properties are prior knowledge. Applying them to missing rectilinear boundary lengths is the unsupported component; calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Move the complete, standalone p14-q9 question to the L-shapes exercise after p17-guided. Keep its prompt and diagrams together.

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter the overlapping-rectangle problem after learning to derive missing rectilinear sides.

findings.finding: The final rectangle arrangement jumps from finding one unknown to coordinating two unknown dimensions against two overall spans.
findings.breakdown: Students must interpret rotated tiles, count contributions to both spans, and choose dimensions satisfying both constraints. Earlier questions establish separate horizontal and vertical totals and inverse perimeter calculations, but do not bridge their simultaneous use.
findings.checked: Checked p16-identify, p17-guided and the complete supplied L-shapes exercise. p18-q2-b has two unknowns determined independently; p20-q6 has one unknown per question. No existing question provides the missing bridge. Although p20-q7 closes the exercise, preceding questions do not build towards coordinating two coupled constraints. p20-q6-c itself needs no repair.
findings.assumptions: Basic equation solving is prior knowledge; simultaneous modelling is not assumed. The proposed trial route needs no calculator.

repair.proposal: Add to p20-q7-root: “Call the short side w and the long side l. Count how many short and long sides make the full width, then do the same for the full height. Try w = 1, 2, 3 cm. For each trial, use the 30 cm width to find l, then check the 31 cm height.” The resulting constraints are 6w + 2l = 30 and 2w + 3l = 31; w = 2 cm and l = 9 cm satisfy both.

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route for generating dimensions from one span and checking the other, while still counting the tile contributions themselves.

findings.finding: The first guided question supplies the perimeter equation instead of requiring the modelling decision taught by the example.
findings.breakdown: The printed P = 3 + 4 + x lets students fill the numerical blanks without translating the diagram into an equation.
findings.checked: p22-teaching identifies writing the equation as step 1, and p22-example-demonstration models it. p22-guided-a supplies that expression repeatedly. Parts b and c restore the decision later, but do not remedy its removal from the first practice.
findings.assumptions: The first guided question practises the stated four-step method. Calculator availability does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Replace the supplied equation chain with: “Write an equation by adding all three side lengths. Substitute the perimeter, simplify, then solve for x.” Retain working lines headed P =, 12 =, 12 = and x =, leaving their right-hand sides blank.

findings.doneWhen: Students construct the side-sum expression before substituting and solving.

findings.finding: Extend the common-perimeter question to explore how rectangle dimensions compensate for one another.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a fixed perimeter with a fixed sum of length and width.
findings.checked: The regular hexagon has perimeter 6 × 4 = 24 cm. Rectangles with lengths 8 cm and 9 cm therefore have widths 4 cm and 3 cm. Rectangle perimeter and finding unknown sides are available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: Optional further parts use the common perimeter established in p24-q7.

repair.proposal: Append to p24-q7: '(a) A rectangle has the same perimeter as these polygons and length 8 cm. Find its width. (b) Another rectangle has the same perimeter and length 9 cm. Find its width. (c) Explain why increasing the length by 1 cm reduced the width by 1 cm.' Expected answers: (a) 4 cm; (b) 3 cm; (c) length and width must still add to 12 cm because each occurs twice in the 24 cm perimeter.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts retain the existing 24 cm perimeter and ask one question per part.

findings.finding: The angular-distance question uses fractional revolutions before instruction connects a rotation angle with the number of circumferences travelled.
findings.breakdown: Knowing one circumference and handling whole laps does not supply the conversion from 4230° to 4230/360 revolutions.
findings.checked: The preceding circumference teaching models complete circles. p36-q7 and p37-q10 use whole laps or turns; p37-q11 reverses distance and revolutions. None connects degrees with fractional turns. The arc-length teaching that supplies the connection comes later.
findings.assumptions: Students know a full turn is 360°. A calculator is assumed, consistent with p35-q3 and the requested decimal answer.

repair.proposal: Add to p38-q12: “One revolution is 360°. Divide the total angle by 360° to find the number of revolutions, including any fraction, then multiply by the distance travelled in one revolution.”

findings.doneWhen: Students have the angle-to-revolutions connection while still choosing the radius, converting units and calculating distance.

findings.finding: Guided part c first requires deriving the target arc's angle from a supplied exterior angle without prompting that decision.
findings.breakdown: Students can continue the preceding substitution pattern using 210°, although the selected arc subtends 150°.
findings.checked: p40-q1 explicitly supplies internal angles. p41 establishes the selected angle-to-arc relationship, but neither it nor p42-example-demonstration and p42-guided-a/b models deriving that angle from an exterior angle. The general definition does not demonstrate the new numerical decision.
findings.assumptions: Students know angles around a point total 360°; they need a cue connecting that knowledge to the selected arc.

repair.proposal: Before the calculation in p42-guided-c, add: 'θ is the angle subtended by the selected arc. First find θ = 360° − 210° = ____.'

findings.doneWhen: Students identify and calculate the selected arc's 150° central angle before substitution.

findings.finding: Extend the existing lane calculation to expose the constant increase in semicircular bend length.
findings.breakdown: A further lane makes the additional distance from each one-metre radius increase visible.
findings.checked: Lane 3 has route length 85.332 + 38.5π ≈ 206.28 m. Its difference from lane 1 is 2π ≈ 6.28 m. Each successive one-metre radius increase adds π metres. All required methods are available.
findings.assumptions: Use the question's stated lane-radius model and retain unrounded values when finding differences.

repair.proposal: After p44-q5-c append: '(d) Lane 3 has radius 38.5 m and the same 85.332 m straight. Calculate its route length to 2 decimal places. (e) How much farther along the route should lane 3 start than lane 1 so both runners travel the same distance? (f) Explain why each successive lane needs approximately another 3.14 m of stagger.' Expected answers: (d) 206.28 m; (e) 6.28 m; (f) each one-metre radius increase adds π metres to the semicircular bend while the straight stays unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts extend the existing track context and separate calculation, comparison and explanation.

findings.finding: Hold arc length fixed while doubling the central angle to expose the resulting halving of radius.
findings.breakdown: The existing questions change both arc length and angle, so they do not isolate this relationship.
findings.checked: Using r = 180l/(πθ), the proposed radii are 11.46 m, 5.73 m, 2.86 m and 7.88 m. Every angle and length is valid, and the inverse-operation method is supplied in p45.
findings.assumptions: Students use calculators and round only their final answers.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p48-q7-c, under its existing instruction, add the single instruction line 'Predict how the radius will change before calculating.' Add (d) arc length 6 m, angle 30°; (e) arc length 6 m, angle 60°; (f) arc length 6 m, angle 120°. Answers: 11.46 m, 5.73 m, 2.86 m. Follow with unpatterned part (g): arc length 11 m, angle 80°; answer 7.88 m. Arc length and units stay fixed in d–f while the angle doubles.

findings.doneWhen: Three consecutive parts isolate angle changes at fixed arc length, followed by one unpatterned part.

findings.finding: Move the junction between the smaller semicircles while retaining the large semicircle.
findings.breakdown: Students compare concrete unequal diameter pairs whose sum stays 18 m and discover that the complete perimeter stays unchanged.
findings.checked: For smaller diameters 6 m and 12 m, or 4 m and 14 m, their combined arc length is 9π m. The large arc is also 9π m, so each complete perimeter is 18π m. The smaller arcs remain within their respective diameter spans and form valid boundaries.
findings.assumptions: Retain one outward and one inward smaller semicircle, and keep the large diameter at 18 m.

repair.proposal: Append to p56-q3-b: '(i) Keep the large semicircle, but change the smaller semicircle diameters to 6 m and 12 m. Find the exact perimeter. (ii) Change the smaller diameters to 4 m and 14 m. Find the exact perimeter. (iii) Explain why the perimeters in (i) and (ii) are equal.' Expected answers: (i) 18π m; (ii) 18π m; (iii) the smaller diameters total 18 m in both cases, so their arcs total 9π m, while the large arc remains 9π m.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up retains the existing shape structure and presents one question in each part.

findings.finding: The circumference review omits numerical substitution, which both introductory examples use directly.
findings.breakdown: Simplifying multiplication notation does not check whether students can replace the correct variable with its given value and write the resulting expression.
findings.checked: p31-q2 simplifies expressions without substituting values. p22-teaching and p22-example establish substitution earlier, but the immediately preceding circle-features topic rehearses geometric identification rather than substitution.
findings.assumptions: Substitution is prior learning whose fluent recall the opening review should check. The repair does not depend on calculator use.

repair.proposal: Append: “First substitute the given values, then evaluate: (a) 3x when x = 4; (b) 2y when y = 2.8; (c) 2ab when a = 3 and b = 5.” Expected working: 3 × 4 = 12; 2 × 2.8 = 5.6; 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. These three short items fit within a one-page review.

findings.doneWhen: The review checks numerical substitution before the circumference examples use it.

findings.finding: Finding radius has no opening review of division to isolate an unknown multiplied by a complete coefficient.
findings.breakdown: Both examples require undoing multiplication; the radius example requires dividing by the entire 2π coefficient.
findings.checked: Earlier p21-q3-c and p21-q3-e rehearse multiplicative equations, so this is prior knowledge rather than missing teaching. It is absent from this topic's opening and from the immediately preceding arc-length review and exercise, which chiefly substitute and evaluate.
findings.assumptions: One-step multiplicative equations are prior learning. Calculator use is irrelevant to the proposed recall check.

repair.proposal: Before p45-information-block add: “Solve, showing the inverse operation on both sides: (a) 5x = 35; (b) 18 = 3y; (c) 2 × 4 × z = 40. Simplify the multiplier first in (c).” Expected answers: x = 7, y = 6, z = 5. These three items fit comfortably on one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse division on both sides, including a right-hand unknown and a coefficient containing two factors.

findings.finding: Q3 demonstrates Method 1 (move the inside edges out to make a rectangle) only on an L-shape, where the perimeter equals that of the bounding rectangle, and records it as the more efficient method. Q4 then invites students to use the method they prefer on shapes that include notches (4c, 4e), where the bounding rectangle gives the wrong perimeter. Nothing says when Method 1 holds.
findings.breakdown: The plausible wrong rule is 'the perimeter of any shape made of right angles equals the perimeter of the rectangle it fits in'. It gives the right answer for the Q3 L-shape and for the staircases and L-shape in 4a, 4b and 4f, so it is reinforced. On 4c it gives 2(20 + 11) = 62 mm instead of 78 mm, and on 4e it gives 2(10 + 9) = 38 cm instead of 46 cm, because the notch sides are extra length that cannot be pushed out onto the rectangle.
findings.checked: Worked 4c (20 + 11 + 11 + 20 + 4 x 4 = 78 mm) and 4e (10 + 3 + 7 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 7 + 9 = 46 cm); both differ from the bounding rectangle by twice the notch depth. p17-example-content and p17-guided-a to p17-guided-c use only missing sides and never mention the shortcut. p18-q1 and p18-q2 include notch and T shapes but were done before Method 1 was introduced, so no question or teaching contrasts a shape where Method 1 works with one where it fails. Q4 does test the distinction, but practice that needs the general case does not expose a special-case rule.
findings.assumptions: Students take 'Method 1' from Q3 as a general rule. No calculator needed.

repair.proposal: Add one line to the stem of Q4 (or after Q3b): 'Method 1 only works when every inside edge can be moved out onto the rectangle. For each shape, decide first whether it works. If a shape has a notch, the sides of the notch are extra.' Keep the Q3b answer as 'Method 1, for this shape'.

findings.doneWhen: Before attempting Q4, students have been told that Method 1 has a condition, and 4c and 4e are answered as 78 mm and 46 cm either by Method 2 or by the bounding rectangle plus the notch sides.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Q6 gives the perimeter and asks for x, which means writing every side in terms of x, forming an equation and solving it. That method is the subject of the next topic (p22-teaching, p22-example and the equation review at p21) and nothing before Q6 supplies it.
findings.breakdown: Up to Q5 every unknown is found from sums and differences of given side lengths. In Q6 the perimeter is the given, x sits on several sides, and other sides depend on x (5 - x and x + 5 in part a; a width of 3x in part b). Students have no model for 'write the perimeter, set it equal to P, simplify, solve' until the following topic, so they can only guess or add the numbers they can see.
findings.checked: Worked the three parts: a) 20 + 2x = 24, x = 2; b) 8x + 10 = 34, x = 3; c) 4x + 24 = 60, x = 9. All need like terms collected and a two-step equation. p17-example-content, p17-guided-a to p17-guided-c, p18-q1, p18-q2 (x and y only label lengths found by subtraction), p19-q3, p19-q4 and p20-q5-a to p20-q5-c contain no perimeter equation. The method first appears at p22-teaching, and its prerequisite equations are rehearsed at p21-q2-block and p21-q3-block, both after this question.
findings.assumptions: Topics are taught in booklet order. Solving 2x + 20 = 24 is prior knowledge from the algebra booklets; forming the equation from a perimeter is what is new.

repair.proposal: Move Q6 (all three parts) out of the L-shapes exercise and into the Solving perimeter problems exercise, after p25-q10, where the four-step method and an expression-valued side (x + 6) have already been met. If it must stay, add the cue: 'Write each side as a number or in terms of x, add them, and make the total equal to P.'

findings.doneWhen: Students meet Q6 only after the worked example and guided practice on finding a side from a given perimeter, or Q6 carries a cue that states the method.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: A short run that removes first a corner and then a notch from the same rectangle, so students see when the perimeter stays the same as the rectangle's and when it grows.
findings.breakdown: Removing a corner leaves the perimeter unchanged; removing a notch from the middle of a side adds twice the notch depth. This is the condition for Method 1 in Q3 and prepares Q4c and Q4e.
findings.checked: 10 by 8 rectangle: 36 cm. Corners removed: 36 cm each. Notch 3 wide and 2 deep: 36 + 4 = 40 cm. Notch 3 wide and 4 deep: 36 + 8 = 44 cm. Corner plus a notch 3 deep: 36 + 6 = 42 cm. Needs only missing sides and addition, both taught by p17.

repair.proposal: Start with a 10 cm by 8 cm rectangle (P = 36 cm). Before calculating, predict whether each change makes the perimeter larger, smaller or the same. a) Remove a 3 cm by 2 cm corner [36 cm]. b) Remove a 5 cm by 6 cm corner [36 cm]. c) Remove a notch 3 cm wide and 2 cm deep from the middle of the top edge [40 cm]. d) Remove a notch 3 cm wide and 4 cm deep from the middle of the top edge [44 cm]. What varies: where the piece is removed and how deep it is. What stays the same: the 10 cm by 8 cm rectangle. Then one unpatterned question: a 10 cm by 8 cm rectangle with a 2 cm by 3 cm corner removed and a notch 4 cm wide and 3 cm deep removed from the bottom edge [42 cm]. Placement: after Q3 and before Q4.

findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: A short run on one rectangle where a semicircle is first added outward and then cut inward, to show that both arcs count and are the same length.
findings.breakdown: Students see that an arc cut into a shape is still part of its boundary and is as long as the same arc bulging out, which Q2f and Q2h rely on.
findings.checked: Rectangle 10 by 6: 32.0 cm. Semicircle of diameter 10 replacing the top edge, outward or inward: 10 + 6 + 6 + 5 pi = 37.7 cm. Semicircle of diameter 6 replacing the right side: 10 + 10 + 6 + 3 pi = 35.4 cm. Follow-up: 12 + 7 + 7 + 6 + 3 pi = 32 + 3 pi = 41.4 cm. Needs only the method of p54.

repair.proposal: Every shape starts from a rectangle 10 cm wide and 6 cm tall. Predict first: 'Which shape has the longest perimeter? Which two are the same?' Then calculate, to 1 d.p.: A) the rectangle [32.0 cm] B) the top edge replaced by a semicircle of diameter 10 cm bulging out [37.7 cm] C) the top edge replaced by a semicircle of diameter 10 cm cut into the rectangle [37.7 cm] D) the right side replaced by a semicircle of diameter 6 cm bulging out [35.4 cm]. What varies: the direction and position of the semicircle. What stays the same: the rectangle. Then one unpatterned question: a rectangle 12 cm by 7 cm with a semicircular notch of diameter 6 cm cut into the middle of its top edge [32 + 3 pi = 41.4 cm]. Placement: between Q2e and Q2f.

findings.finding: Find the angle at which a sector's arc length equals its radius, and show that its perimeter is then 3r for every radius.
findings.breakdown: Students return to P = l + 2r and the arc-length formula and find that the angle does not depend on the radius.
findings.checked: (theta / 360) x 2 pi r = r gives theta = 360 / (2 pi) = 57.3 degrees to 1 d.p., with r cancelling for any r > 0; then P = r + 2r = 3r. Solving for the angle is already required by p51-q7, so the method is available by the end of the topic.

repair.proposal: A sector has an arc length equal to its radius. a) Find its angle, correct to 1 decimal place. b) Does the angle depend on the radius? Explain. c) Show that its perimeter is 3r. Expected answer: a) (theta / 360) x 2 pi r = r, so theta = 360 / (2 pi), about 57.3 degrees. b) No, r cancels from both sides. c) P = l + 2r = r + 2r = 3r. Placement: at the end of the exercise, after Q9, for students who finish early.

contextQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students learnt that a sector occupying three eighths of a circle's area also has three eighths of its circumference? The separate area booklet could supply this knowledge, but the supplied teaching does not establish whether students have encountered it; the answer determines whether p51-q6 needs a connecting cue.
